utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Prosecution for the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Vos on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Toma Fila and together with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic I am defending Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Thank you. Thank you. Before we start, I would like to express the gratitude of the bench to the Prosecution for filing yesterday two additional legal briefs which will prove, I am sure, very helpful. We would be much obliged to the Prosecution if we could also be handed in the legal authorities supporting their legal briefs. I wonder whether it is complicated. It is just a way of helping the court, and of course it will be for Mr. Fila to decide whether to address these two issues, namely international versus internal armed conflict and the question of accumulation of charges in his opening statement or in additional briefs, but in any case, again, we would be grateful to him if at some point in time he would be so kind as to hand in the legal authorities supporting his views on this matter. All right. I wonder whether... no? Yes? Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Witness A, the witness that we have intended to call for the last day or so, is still quite ill, and in fact had to return to the doctor last night after coughing up blood. He is here. He is running quite a high fever, and is really in no condition to testify. I spoke with Mr. Fila beforehand, and he kindly agreed that if the witness would come in we can identify his statement, and introduce that and then we would seek to introduce his testimony from the Rule 61 hearing and then allow him to leave, if your Honours are agreeable with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So then you are referring both to the written statement and the Rule 61 transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether Mr. Fila agrees, or would you like to cross-examine, not today, probably, because in this case we could maybe ask the witness to come back in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no intention to cross-examine him at all. He is not speaking of my defendant at all, because it is better to have a court official go and see him rather than have a sick man testify over here, so why does not the official go there and identify him and that is fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. At this time if we can just have him brought in we will have him identify the statement and very quickly deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just while we have a moment, when the witness is being brought in, your Honours, we filed yesterday -- I see the witness. I will raise it later. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration? WITNESS A (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like for you to examine this piece of paper, please, and, sir, at this time I am going to hand you a small piece of paper and if you can look at this and tell me if that is your name indicated on this sheet of paper, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would seek to tender this as Prosecutor's exhibit...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: 78. Thank you. And this would be tendered under seal. Sir, while you are in court today I will be referring to you as, "Witness A". Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In August 1995 do you recall meeting with Mr. Vladimir Dzuro, an investigator from the Tribunal Office of the Prosecutor and myself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at that time did you give a statement which was taken down in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was that statement subsequently read back to you by an interpreter into the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show the witness a document that we are marking as Prosecutor's Exhibit 79, and a Croatian translation of that document which will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 79A. Looking at the document that we have marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 79, do you see your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you indicate that this was your -- that this statement was true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would tender that as Prosecutor's Exhibit 79, and 79A, the Croatian translation, both under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Fila? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Witness A, do you recall coming to this court in March of 1996 and testifying in a proceeding which is known as a Rule 61 hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, so I see that there is no objection to the witness being released. Witness A, I would like on behalf of the court to express to you our gratitude for coming here and I am so sorry that you are not well and I hope that you will soon recover. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek to introduce the testimony from the Rule 61 hearing as Prosecutor's Exhibit 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Prosecution calls Petr Kypr. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration? PETR KYPR (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, is your full name Petr Kypr?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you recall on 15th March 1996 being interviewed by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, Mr. Vladimir Dzuro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of that -- was that interview recorded in the Czech language with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the original was written in Czech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you sign the original in the Czech language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign all the pages of this document in Czech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that it has subsequently been translated into the English language and into the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I have seen the English version. And in the English version, if I may add, I found one mistake on page 6, and I would like you now to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, we will come to that in a moment. Firstly, I would like to show you these exhibits, these documents, and could they be marked with the Prosecution number next in order and then A and B, A for the English version, B for the Croatian version, the original exhibit being in the Czech language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kypr, I am just asking you, if you would, look at the statement in the Czech language and tell me if you see your signature appearing at the foot of each page of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree this is the copy of the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And now, you were telling us a moment ago that you -- in the English version -- you found a small error that you would like to correct. Perhaps before we move onto that, I understand that you speak English. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand English, I can speak some English but I was recommended to use the interpreter here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I am only asking you that for the purposes -- that you can point in the English translation to the error. So perhaps you might take us there. Page 6, and where is the error?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is page 6, as I said, the first paragraph. It is the sixth line from the bottom, "Dr. Bosanac", and there in the brackets we have, "(who)" -- sorry, no, there is a wrong translation in Serbian. Behind the word, "Bosanac", we have something added, and what has been added here is the beginning of the bracket, and then the word, "who".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, just to cover that, it is the sixth line on the first paragraph, page 6, after the highlighted word, "Bosanac", there appears a bracket and the word, "who", and you are saying that neither the bracket nor the word, "who", should appear there and should be deleted to make a better understanding of the sentence. Thank you. I tender those statements, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now it is okay and as far as I know in the Serbian transcription the text is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, in 1991 were you appointed a Monitor for the European Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the late summer, at the end of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after your appointment, where did you take up position? Where did you take up your duty as a Monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I was in Zagreb where I worked in different positions. I was stationed in Slovenia and Dalmatia and Gosbitzedal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what position did you hold as an European Monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was appointed by the Czech government, the head of the Czech delegation in the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what position did you have in the mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zagreb, because I speak Serbo-Croatian, I was in the team of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what about when you went to Belgrade? What position did you hold there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mission soon realised that it was also important to set up regional centres, that is in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, and what position did you have in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and I was sent to Belgrade as the representative of the Head of the Belgrade centre, as the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, as -- in your role as deputy head of mission in Belgrade, were you exposed to a number of documents that were documents of the ECMM and documents that the ECMM received from various parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was my duty, because (a) I could speak both English and Serbo-Croat, and (b) I was also the deputy head of the mission. In other words, I was a member of the mission, that is the one of the team consisting of Mr. Perrin, myself, and the head of the Monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In late September, early October of 1991 did you receive a directive to have regard to what was occurring in Ilok, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We got instructions from Zagreb -- I am sorry, could you please turn up the volume on my headset? Yes, we got instructions from the Zagreb centre to send a team to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was a team subsequently sent to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One member of the team was sent to Ilok and I was not in that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you then subsequently go to Ilok yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Ilok. I believe this was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did you get to Ilok? Can you describe to the court the procedures you went through and the course that you took to arrive at Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The standard procedure for all these trips or travels of Monitors' teams to the front-line from Belgrade was as follows: we had a vehicle for Monitors and it was accompanied by another vehicle of the liaison officer of the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the Yugoslav People's Army or national army, how far did you go? Did you go all the way into Ilok or did you go only part of the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had to cover roughly 130 kilometres. It took us three hours, and we had to stop before the bridge to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, where is this bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While the liaison officer had to establish contact with the local command of the Yugoslav national army to let us cross the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where is the bridge? In what town was this bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the bridge between Backa Palanka, which is on the Serbian side, and Ilok which is on the Croatian side of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you, after contact was made with Ilok, did you then subsequently go into Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We went into Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened when you got into Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked to the representatives of that town who described the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they informed us that the Yugoslav army demanded that they surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did they speak to you about plans for evacuation of the people of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that they were considering evacuation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did they ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but that it had not been decided whether there would be a referendum on this in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they show you any documentation, in relation to discussions that they had had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had been shown the proposal submitted by the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you read this proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I ask you to look at this document that I now show you, one being in the Croat language, Serbo-Croat language, one being in English. Perhaps it might be marked the next Prosecution exhibit in order, and the English version of it be given the letter A. Do you recognise the documents which you are now being shown? I have a copy there for the Defence, and the judges, apparently. There is only one page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb version does correspond to what I recollect. I have not looked at the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. I am just talking about the version that you were handed. When you saw this document, what were the most significant features of it, so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was an obvious offer to take over control of the town. This corresponds to item 6, accompanied by certain sanctions in case of problems arising. That is item 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what role, if any, was the ECMM to play in the course of this evacuation, so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The European Union Mission had very limited possibilities, given in the memorandum of understanding, and these meant that we were allowed to monitor the situation and only on restricted territory, that is on the territory of Croatia, not of Serbia. We were also allowed to communicate between the two parties and to help achieve an armistice and also possibly to try to prevent bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall at this time the name or names of any of the JNA personnel that you had dealings with during the course of these discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the local commander was Colonel Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the JNA, were there any other parties on the Serb side with whom you had dealings in connection with this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall talking to any civilians about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your evidence that there was discussion about a referendum in Ilok about this so-called evacuation. Were you aware of whether or not such a referendum was held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were there on the 12th and we were told that on the 13th there would be this referendum, and if I remember it correctly, our team arrived there on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know the outcome of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were informed by the municipality at Ilok about the results of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you recall what the outcome of the referendum was? I am not asking for specific details, but do you recall what the outcome of the referendum was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimously -- there were two questions asked under the referendum. One question was whether, due to the crisis situation, they should leave the town, and the other question asked in the referendum was whether they should surrender all the weapons and sign a treaty with the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the evacuation to take place, planned to take place, of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is one thing I should like to add, and that is we had been informed about the outcome, so the result concerning the first question about the evacuation, it was decided that the majority of the citizens of Ilok wanted to be evacuated, wanted to leave, but at the same time, as for the second question, they did not want to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when was this evacuation scheduled to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I think it was to be on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you attend the evacuation yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That day I had to leave in the morning. I had to leave for Belgrade, for Belgrade, and that is why I saw only the very beginning of forming the evacuation column, and it was a very sad picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, might the witness be shown Exhibit P5 for a moment, please? Looking for me at that document, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, or rather I recognise this document in its Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right, yes. Now, when did you see that document that you -- Exhibit P5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember it correctly, this was on the 14th October. When we arrived at Ilok, the municipality informed us that it had to respect the results of the referendum and to arrange for the evacuation with the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you will see, I think, that article 3 of that document refers to 17th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this was when the mines were being removed from the surroundings of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And article 8 makes mention that after that, on 17th October, the convoy will depart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from -- perhaps that exhibit can be returned to the Registrar -- apart from inspecting Ilok itself, were you requested to also inspect surrounding villages and other places around Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation at Ilok and in its surroundings was very dramatic because Ilok was at the very apex of the triangle which, in fact, was under siege by the Yugoslav national army and at Ilok at the same time there were a number of refugees from villages surrounding Ilok, including some people from Vukovar, and also from villages like Opatovac, Lovas, Sarengrad, Bapska and I cannot remember the names of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 16th October 1991 did you have occasion to visit the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We visited a number of villages surrounding this town, and one of them was also Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, at this time when you went to Lovas, had it been conquered or taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The village was taken over, had been taken over, and we were told this by Serb volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you were told that the village had been taken by Serb volunteers. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A representative of that village had told us so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the village, did you meet with the local commander of the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were received in the presence of some ten other citizens of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the local military commander that you met, he was a Serb, was he, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at least he said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in addition to being the local military commander, did he claim to have any other title?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he told us that the village is now in the command of five people, and he is the head of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say what his position was, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if I remember it correctly, he said he was the military commander and he also said he was a -- what would be a mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The mayor of the town. Did he say to you why it was necessary that Lovas was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He explained to us that the attack was necessary because in the village there was a Serb minority that was being threatened by the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he speak of the need to change the ethnic balance in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, elaborate just a little bit more on that. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was rather surprising, because he was saying that it was essential that Serb people were moved into the village from other areas, and to change the structure that is unnatural because there was this majority of Croats, but honestly, I do not know whether I remember this correctly because we are talking about a time seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say whether the JNA had played any role in the taking of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and this again surprised us, because he said that he had invested money in equipment, that he had provided equipment for the unit that had liberated the village, that he had invested I cannot remember how many Deutschmarks. I honestly cannot remember how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From the observations you made in this region, and having regard to the attacks on the various villages that you witnessed, did you form any view as to the approach that was being taken by the forces on the Serb side in relation to the military tactics of both the JNA, the volunteers and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was interesting, perhaps, was that the Yugoslav army rather held positions in the area where these villages were located and there were groups that we referred to as, "paramilitary groups", at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and what did the paramilitary groups do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I get the Serb translation, please? The last question has not been translated into Serbian: please repeat once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What role did the paramilitary groups play, so far as you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the forces of the first attack, but this is a matter of what we were told, in fact, because in view of the rules under which we operated, we were never in the areas where paramilitary operations were proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you subsequently become involved in the evacuation of the town or city of Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the fall of the city was being expected, and it was important to ensure humanitarian operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time are we talking about? What month and date are we talking about now, when you say that the fall of the town was expected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking roughly about one month after the events at Ilok. In other words, we are talking about the period between 15th November and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, how did you become aware of the necessity for the ECMM to become involved in this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a common procedure adopted by the European Union Mission, when our teams, to provide for the crossings of the frontiers for, let us say delegations from the two parties or for the humanitarian convoys of the two parties...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, you can speak normally. The translation will keep up with you fairly well. If you are moving too fast, they will tell us. You can just speak normally. You do not need to stop to allow the -- and do not be concerned about what is happening on the television screen in front of you. You do not have to keep pace with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. The European Mission was to provide for the transfer of convoys, in other words, by keeping the mandate. It had, in other words -- we were making sure that the rules of a cease-fire were being honoured. A typical example was at Vukovar where the European Mission in fact was involved in providing conditions for a number of convoys that were leaving Vukovar because there were not only the two convoys from the Vukovar hospital, but there were also other convoys. Citizens of Vukovar, and each of these columns in fact was accompanied by one or more teams from the EUMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where was the -- you mentioned the hospital, as a point of evacuation in Vukovar. Were there any other areas in Vukovar where evacuations were to take place from, so far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, yes, that there were teams from Belgrade who were involved in providing conditions for the evacuation from the centre for refugees that were in the upper part of Vukovar. I cannot remember correctly, but I think it was called Velepromet, the place was called Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And with respect to the evacuation from the hospital in particular, were you aware of whether or not this was to be based on an agreement entered into between the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, orally and then also in a fax we were informed about the contents of the agreement between the Yugoslav national army and the Croat representatives concerning the course of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was the fax sent to you from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, the first piece of information they got by telephone and then this was followed by the fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in addition to a message that you received in -- a facsimile message that you received, did you also receive a copy of an agreement that had been concluded between the parties on the 18th November in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will show you the document. Would you now look at this document for me, please? There is a copy for the Defence, a copy for their Honours and one to become an exhibit. Perhaps it might be given the next exhibit number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the record, your Honours, the attached agreement is Exhibit P9 to this document. Mr. Kypr, do you recognise that as the facsimile message that you have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the message itself, do you know -- this message was sent from Zagreb to your office in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does it say there, and perhaps you might take us to it, the date and time that the evacuation from the hospital was to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is under article 1, where it says that they met on the 18th of November. In the Serb translation it is mentioned that it was the Yugoslav national army and the Croatian, not us as the mission. That was not correctly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say, "Serbian". I think this is only in English, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to the Serb translation that I was getting through the headset.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Oh. Yes. I am asking you to go to the message itself, not the agreement. The message itself. I am asking you there, can you point out, if you look at the second paragraph, number 2, does that say when the evacuation would take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it does not. At least I cannot see it. I cannot see any date here or any minute mentioned, because this was a question of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, would you please look at the message, not the agreement itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are not speaking about message. Sorry. Sorry, you were referring to the message. I see now. It says that, under article 1, that the evacuation of the hospital at Vukovar should start -- should take place on the 20th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 the reference on that, to paragraph 2, 20th, at 8 o'clock in the morning. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also we have the hour here, 0800 hours. That is the military record from the American representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour. Now, I tender that. Perhaps that might be handed back to the Registrar. Mr. Kypr, what role was the ECMM to play in this evacuation, so far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already stated, the role was to monitor the armistice rules and also all the agreements that we have also seen in the annex of the document that I had submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on where in Vukovar, because as for the upper part of Vukovar there we arrived at roughly 8 o'clock, if I have remember correctly. Then we had a very short briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who gave you this briefing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then, together with the convoy, we went down to the lower part of Vukovar. The briefing, again if I remember it correctly, was given by one of the representatives of the Yugoslav national army, I believe it was Major Sljivancanin. I think it was Major Sljivancanin. I cannot remember any other name or any other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did the briefing take place in Vukovar? Was it at the hospital or was it in the middle of the town, or...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was in the upper part of the town of Vukovar. Perhaps it might have been even in the village on the outskirts, Negoslavci. It was either in the upper part of the town of Vukovar or in one of the neighbouring villages but it was definitely in the upper part that had been under the Serb forces for some time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this was 8 o'clock in the morning on the 18th November -- sorry, on 20th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were you told at this briefing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that it would be made possible for us to take part in the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened next? Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Translation not received)... Followed by the vehicle of the Red Cross. First it was the military command that was followed by the International Red Cross then we had the liaison officer's vehicle, followed by the European Mission's vehicle, followed by some other vehicles, and these were transporters provided by the Yugoslav army. The whole convoy then proceeded to the lower part of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you got to the lower part of Vukovar, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There we stopped before the bridge over the Vuka River, and we were told that we could not cross, that we could not proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did he tell you why you could not proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that there were mines and that they were currently removing the mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you able to see the hospital from this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not, because in front of us there was some military vehicles, and if I remember the situation in the town well, the hospital had some other buildings in front of it, so we were not able to see the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you at the time concerned about this delay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we were used to it because this was a standard procedure. We would be told that there are certain places that we could not access for security reasons, and again, following the rules of the European Union, we had to respect this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long were you held up at this bridge over the Vuka River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about two hours, until 10.30, quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At about 10.30, 10.45, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were allowed to proceed and we arrived at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin or somebody else from the JNA tell you that the road had now been cleared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember who it was who told us. It was just that the columns started moving. I cannot remember. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you reached the hospital, what did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First we saw the situation in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very sad situation where the hospital -- in fact, as we were told, the hospital, in fact, had been without electricity, without water for three months, and people were in underground areas, under the hospital. As for the situation around the hospital, next to the hospital there was a group of people in civilian clothes, and we were told that this is the hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you whether or not other patients had already been removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were told both by the patients and by the hospital staff that we met in the hospital. They told us that some of the patients had already been taken away and also some of the doctors had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they say which of the patients had been taken away already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember anybody specifying any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But did they... okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for names, I know that Dr. Bosanac was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am not after names. I am asking were they any particular type of patient or persons that had been removed. Were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had been told that these are the patients that the Yugoslav army had suspected of being Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you to look at this document that I now show you. I have a copy for your Honours, a copy for the Defence, and one that might be marked as an exhibit, and might the document be placed on the ELMO screen, and Mr. Kypr, I am going to ask you to look at the document on the overhead projector beside you, and to tell us what this document is, and point out to us various features of it, if you would be so kind. When you are speaking, can I ask you to turn your head to the microphone, when you actually answer, because you need to make sure that your voice is picked up, so it is a bit of an awkward position to be in but I would ask you to do that for me, and, just pointing with a pointer to the document in front of you, firstly, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a sketch that I made for the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is it a sketch of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the situation in the hospital when we arrived. I noticed one thing that I considered rather unusual, and that is that at two places there were small heaps of sharp objects like penknives, for example, scissors, and most of these were just scissors and penknives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you mark on this particular document that is now displayed the locations of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two small heaps, one was near to the entrance to the hospital, and the second here in this location, (indicates) it was on a hospital trolley that was just standing there, somewhere nearby, nearby, again, not far from the entrance to the hospital. There was an underground, or there is an entrance to the underground premises of the hospital which was used as the main entrance at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this document is drawn by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have drawn this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the writing that appears on it is your writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And might the witness be shown exhibit -- well, might I be given Exhibit P8? I wish to show the witness a photograph. Just looking at the photograph that now appears on the projector beside you, which is part of Exhibit P8, could you, on that photograph, point to the same locations where you found this small heap of sharp objects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first heap was somewhere here in this location, here, on the lawn, or on this concrete pavement, and the other one was somewhere here, and this was the trolley that was standing here on this path. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is the entrance to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And for the record, your Honour, that is the fifth photograph of P8. Thank you. That might be taken back to the Registrar. Thank you. Mr. Kypr, did you raise the issue of the absence of these people that had been taken away with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They did this through our liaison officer, because this, again, was a standard procedure. First we addressed the liaison officer and it was up to him to respond to this, but we were given no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay at the hospital until the people were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Together with Dr. Schou, we joined the first convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did the remainder of the people that you saw at the hospital when you arrived, when did their evacuation commence on that day, 20th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can talk about the group of people that we saw standing next to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did it first commence, the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And as far as I remember, these -- the evacuation of these commenced immediately after our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two ways -- I mean, two groups. One was the Serb group and the other one was the Croats who wanted to be evacuated together with our convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what time did the Serb group, what time were they evacuated? Are you able to give you... was it midday, later in the afternoon? Are you able to give us any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say this precisely. I think it must have been in the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the group that wanted to go to Croatia, what time did their evacuation commence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was postponed until soon after lunch because there were some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some problems of a logistical nature, for example, who would be taken out first, because the hospital was overcrowded, the corridors were very narrow, it was difficult to carry the wounded and the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So when these logistical problems were overcome, what time did the evacuation of the Croatian people commence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, the whole convoy with the wounded and also a number of buses, I believe there were three or five buses, I cannot remember, these were ready at about 3.30 or 4 o'clock in the afternoon and then immediately after that the convoy set out on the journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did they go? Did you accompany the convoy all the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our vehicle was part of the convoy where these wounded were transported, and also the buses were -- we went to Sremska Mitrovica because on the front-line it was impossible to get a crossing, because it was being fired on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, when you talked about Lovas, you mentioned the mayor. Is Lovas a village or a town? It does not have a population of 2,000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since when do villages have mayors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a misinterpretation in the transcription, because I did state that he introduced himself to us as the military representative of the village, and also as a civilian representative of the village, and he said he was a chief of a five member council that was representing the village, but I do not remember the exact title he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is a question of interpretation. "Mayor", in our language, "gradonacolink", mentions, "grad", town, so it is the head of a town, and Mr. Niemann has been using the expression, "mayor". The convoy that left on 20th November from Vukovar, several convoys that left, were there any members of the Croat army who had been disarmed and were then safely sent to Croatia? I mean not from the hospital but from outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question because I was only in the hospital. In other words, I can provide evidence on what I saw myself, and if I remembered correctly, these people were not there, or at least they were not observed by us. We were taking care of the patients who were in the hospital and also the staff and some of the members of the staff who were in the hospital and around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, before the 20th November were there only patients who were civilians at the hospital or were there also wounded members of the Croatian army or the paramilitary armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had been told that there were also members of the Croat army, which is quite easy to understand because we are talking about a military front.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Among the people about whom you were told that they were taken away, were there civilians or were there members of the military or were there both, one or the other? Did anybody give you an explanation as to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not remember anything of this. Nobody had specified to us what was the composition of the group that had been taken away. We were told that those people had been taken away who -- about whom it was believed that they were the members of the Croat army, and also some doctors had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You do not know whether that was true or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us who told you about these people who were taken away and who had taken them away, and where were they taken away? Do you know more about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know anything about this. I do not know why these people had been taken away, because we had other obligations to see to, and as for who told us, there was no light, remember this, so the people we were talking about, we could hardly see them and the situation was very dramatic and I cannot remember the identities of the people that we talked to, but we were told by more people, both by the patients and by the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But what? Did an official tell you something to that effect, for example, Major Sljivancanin, a captain or a lieutenant, someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, and thank you for your time. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you like to re-examine? No. Thank you. Thank you. I assume there is no objection to the witness being dismissed. Mr. Kypr, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be dismissed. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. That is the evidence that we have for this month. Your Honours, we filed a motion yesterday, Mr. Fila is aware of it. It is a motion in relation to the taking of a deposition of a witness in Vukovar. It is in a sense -- I understand the Defence have no objection to this course, but it is a matter that we would like your Honours ruling on, notwithstanding that it would be by consent, I think, between the parties, but whether your Honours have had a chance to see this or not yet, it was filed late yesterday. I do not know whether it is convenient to look at it at some time today, if your Honour has had some time, or whether your Honours would want more time to consider it. The course proposed in it is not dissimilar to that which is being proposed in another case, of Aleksovski and the terms of the proposal are much the same, so it is not something which is totally new to the Tribunal, but it is something which we would need to raise with your Honours and for your Honours to rule on it one way or the other, but this deals with a witness who refuses to testify, and -- in The Hague. He refuses to come to The Hague, and we have attached a copy of his statement to the motion. He is happy to testify in Vukovar, and it seems to us, your Honour, that it is a better course than having to proceed by way of satellite link which is a much more expensive and difficult process. This would be much simpler, and as I understand, Mr. Fila does not object to it, so it would be a course that we would propose. But, your Honours have not had a chance to see it so I am not sure where we can go from here, whether your Honours would like to deal with it today at some stage, later this afternoon, once your Honours have had a chance to consider it, but it would be useful, I think, to hear from Mr. Fila as to what position he has on it. I think he is familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke about this to Mr. Waespi and I said that I would agree to it but I have not seen this document so I do not know what it says. But in principle I wish to state that it is much better if we agree that we read this out as evidence, rather than use the money of this court for a video link that does not really change much. It does not make any difference, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. I understand it is not a question of video link, it is a question of taking a deposition in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I think what Mr. Fila is commenting on is that it is much cheaper to proceed this way rather than have the video link and he is saying that he agrees with it for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So you have no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, but I would like to have a look at it first. Could I see the statement first, please? Nothing else. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The court has decided that we should take a look at the -- at this document and of course this also should be handed to the Defence, maybe in the next half hour, and then we would reconvene, we need at least 30 minutes, and then we could see whether a decision is made, if the Defence has any point to make it is most welcome, and then we will make a ruling, maybe right away. Now, I wonder whether we could also do some planning for March. I understand that the Prosecution will send somebody to Belgrade to interview the various witnesses for the Defence, the 45 people, so that probably some time in March we will know whether or not the Prosecutor is ready to accept the idea of depositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. It probably would not be by -- I do not think it would need to be by deposition. We are having discussions with Mr. Fila today to make an approach on this, and we think that that will perhaps result in a simpler process and then we may only have to interview those that -- where we are unable to reach agreement on certain matters. It is a bit premature for us to say exactly where we are at the moment, but yes, in principle, your Honour is exactly right. We will either proceed to interview all 45 between now and next March when the next sitting is, or alternatively, some other suitable arrangement between the parties could be reached, hopefully. And the same would apply with respect to the settlement of written admissions between the Prosecution and the Defence with respect to our matters, so we will endeavour to reduce the issues to as narrow a point as possible by discussion and by reaching an agreement, if that is possible. So, to answer your Honour, we do expect to be in that position when next we come before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, by when do you think you may be able to know how many witnesses you intend to call? Do you think in March when we start again, when we sit in March you can tell us how many witnesses you intend to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could even tell you now. You know, Mr. Niemann is right. When a trial begins, or rather before it begins, it does not always seem the way it turns out to be. I gave you the statements and addresses of over 117 witnesses. I do not think I am going to be needing even 40 of them. For example, I have a statement of the driver who was mentioned by Witness Q and who took Berghofer, Cakalic and everyone from Ovcara, so it all fits in to what Cakalic, Q and Berghofer said, so I see no reason for him to come here and to say for the fifth time that which we have already heard. I am just giving this as an example, so I am sure that the Prosecutor and I will agree on that. Another example. You know that the indictment says, "around the 20th November". That includes the 19th and the 21st, then. Obviously, the 19th is irrelevant and that there is no need for me to prove Mr. Dokmanovic's alibi for the 19th or for the 21st for that matter, after 1 am, for instance, so that shortens the whole thing as well, so I can tell you in advance that in March the list is truly going to be very shortened. That is the only thing I can tell you, optimistically, and with regard to your first question, in my opening statement I am going to say what I have to say regarding what Mr. Niemann mentioned, that is whether it was an international conflict, an accumulation of charges, et cetera, so these are legal issues, and whether Dokmanovic was there. That is what we are out to prove, so I hope I have made myself clear. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I propose that we stand in recess until 11.30. (10.45 am) (A short break) (11.30 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We apologise for the five minute delay. We needed some time to consult with the Registrar. I wonder whether Mr. Fila has had an opportunity to go through this document. Mr. Fila, would you like to say whether you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection, but I am sorry that such a valuable witness as this one was not examined as fully, as I think was necessary. I promised Mr. Niemann that I would agree with the reading of this document and I do, but I have a proposal, if the Prosecution is agreeable. Perhaps it would be a good idea if the Prosecution take an additional statement from this witness. You see, he talks about an excavator. So far we have been talking about a bulldozer. Perhaps we could take a photograph, whatever it was that was digging the hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just do not want to cut Mr. Fila short, but the whole proposal is that Mr. Fila would have full and ample opportunity to cross-examine this witness, to go down to Vukovar to meet with him, and in proceedings almost identical to what we have here, will have full access to that. It would only be that your Honours would not be there. But we would have a presiding officer. I do not know whether that helps Mr. Fila but he would lose nothing in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. That was just a suggestion on my part. I think it would be useful for all of us here to have a photograph of that excavator, and thank you for this opportunity. I will do my best to interview him. I just thought that we should see what the hole was dug with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Thank you very much for being once again extremely cooperative and helpful. However, the court has problems in granting this request, and there are two questions. We have gone through the various problems which arise in connection with the motion submitted by the Prosecution. There are two problems. One major problem is the presence of the accused. We cannot see how the accused could be present, attend the deposition in Vukovar, and the second problem is a practical set of problems, actually. I would say the practical side is really difficult, and in this respect I would like to ask the senior legal officer who is here with us, to speak on behalf of the Registrar and to, in a way, address the issue of the practical problems that the taking of a deposition would give rise to. Mr.s Featherstone? MR.S FEATHERSTONE: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to stand? Thank you. MR.S FEATHERSTONE: Yes, your Honour. May I, at the same time explain the other option that the Chamber is considering, because you have not actually referred to that yet. I am sure it will be no surprise to the parties that another option for this witness may be to take his evidence via video conference link. Just looking at the practical issues between the two ways of proceeding, for the number of persons who would need to travel to Vukovar, it is essentially the same number that would have to go for a deposition, taking a deposition, as for setting up a video conference link. Indeed, it may even be one additional person because obviously counsel for both sides would need to be present, a presiding officer, interpreters, court reporters, audio visual staff for the recordings, et cetera, and possibly even some security detail assigned to the mission. Therefore, the size of the team that would be required is essentially the same. As regards the possible additional cost of the video conference link itself, I have spoken to the head of the audio visual section at the Tribunal. We do have the equipment for both ends of video-conferencing link, and it would really boil down to the question of whether or not there is a satellite within -- a satellite dish within easy access of the proposed location of hearing the witness. That is something that would need to be investigated, depending on what the parties agreed as to the location of the taking of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you already have all that equipment in Belgrade with Mr. Mehov and it is only an hour's drive from Belgrade to Vukovar so if the Prosecutor agrees, there should be no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether Mr. Niemann could tell us whether the witness would be prepared to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He would like to stay in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but I think there may be the facilities in Vukovar for the satellite link. There is no studio or anything, but I believe that there may be a satellite dish. We are not unduly concerned one way or the other, whether it was done by way of satellite link or whether it is done by way of deposition. So, we are not troubled by that, if the court has a preference, to do it by way of satellite link. Our only concern was that we had discovered in another case that the cost, apparently, was very difficult and that a month's notice was required and there was a whole lot of other difficulties associated with it. It got to the point where we decided that it could not be done in another case, so because of that we proceeded down this route but if that has changed and it now can be done well, we are happy to go back to satellite links. It was done in the Tadic case and done quite successfully, but then when it came to be done in another case it could not be done, so I am not sure what the current status of all that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I ask Mr.s Featherstone to go on, maybe to complete her exposition? MR.S FEATHERSTONE: Thank you. Mr. Niemann is correct there, that the key point will be access to the satellite dish. If that cannot be easily arranged at a suitable location, then that does create difficulties. That is basically the practical aspects of deposition as compared with video-conferencing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (Pause). So, after duly considering the matter and for the reasons I set out before, the court feels that it is not in a position to grant the motion filed by the Prosecution, and prefers to hear the witness through -- by video link, and so therefore we hope that the Registrar can start right away, maybe today, making the necessary preparation for establishing the video link, and we hope that we can hear the witness in March in the week when we are sitting on this case. It is so decided. Thank you. Are there any other matters the parties wished to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. There is a matter that I wish to raise, I am not asking the court to rule on it in any way, I just wish to raise it as an issue, though, so that your Honours are aware of it. We are at the moment, when we have our meeting with Mr. Fila, in the process of reducing the ambit of our evidence as broadly as we can. In doing that, we are considering issues that might be raised in the Defence case. In some jurisdictions there is a practice that the Prosecution must anticipate the Defence case and lead in its own case the evidence which would meet that which is raised, or can reasonably be anticipated to be raised by the Defence in their case. The Rules of the Tribunal, particularly Rule 85(a)(iii), deal with the issue on the basis of the Prosecution presenting further evidence in rebuttal, which to some extent obviates the necessity for the Prosecutor in its case to adduce evidence which would seek to rebut a defence at that stage. We are not expecting, and we do not anticipate that there would be in any way a significant rebuttal case by the Prosecution, but in the process of us reducing our evidence in our own case, we are mindful of the fact that under the Rules we may seek to lead evidence in rebuttal to deal with issues that might arise in the Defence case. Now, there are fine arguments that can be raised that one might anticipate, certain matters being raised in the Defence case, and especially so in this case, because Mr. Fila is being so open in his discovery, so I just wished to note, as it were, that we, in going through this exercise of reducing our evidence, are doing so having regard to the fact that, like in the Tadic case, the Prosecution did call rebuttal evidence, and it is possible and indeed it is probable that we would be seeking to call some rebuttal evidence at that appropriate stage. I am not suggesting it is going to be extensive, but I do expect that we will do that. If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your warning, I think you are right. Under that Rule, yes, you have a right to call rebuttal evidence. Mr. Fila, any comment or would you like to raise any issue? Additional issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think that I never wanted to deny the right of the Prosecution under Rule 85 to call evidence in rebuttal. What we can do to assist would be to see what is controversial, what we are disputing, so that we do not waste any time. I know the Prosecution will not accept that I have an alibi for the defendant, because then there would be no case, but we could, perhaps, agree on some minor things that have already become evident through the testimony. That would shorten the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there are no other matters to transact, and so once again, before we adjourn, let me thank you on behalf of the court, let me thank both parties for their cooperative attitude, and we now stand in recess until March. I hope that meanwhile we may receive some documents from the parties so that we can do some homework on this matter, and we now stand in recess. (11.50 am)
